composition: Nominal composition: 0 at.% Al, i.e. unalloyed iron. The real Al content of this polycrystalline 0 at.% Al reference is listed as n.d. (not determined) in Table 1, so the only quantified composition data are its impurity levels: 100 wt.ppm C; Si and other residual elements are not given for this sample. The general alloy purity target of the study was purity control with every alloy carrying less than 100 wt.ppm C. The reference iron was obtained starting from Fe of 99.99% purity that had been purified by zone melting to minimise the impurity level (the same high-purity Fe used for the vacuum-induction-melted Fe-Al alloys), with the deliberate aim of suppressing the carbide formation and grain-boundary embrittlement associated with the 300–600 wt.ppm C of earlier Fe-Al studies.
conclusions: Pure iron provides the 0 at.% Al anchor point of the study's central result: the room-temperature yield stress of polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al alloys increases linearly with Al content up to 18 at.%, with 21 and 23 MPa per at.% Al at 10⁻² and 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ respectively, and a solid-solution hardening coefficient of about 2.2 GPa insensitive to rate and temperature. The value measured for pure iron (~100 MPa at 10⁻² s⁻¹; between 0 and 100 MPa at 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) therefore quantifies the solute-free baseline against which Al hardening, short-range ordering effects and quench-induced vacancy hardening in the sibling Fe-Al samples are measured. The contrast between this ~2.2 GPa polycrystalline hardening coefficient and the ~1 GPa reported earlier for single-slip monocrystals is attributed to differences in alloy preparation (as-cast polycrystals vs monocrystals annealed at 900 °C for 24 h and air cooled) and in slip mode (multiple slip in polycrystals vs single [111](110) slip in monocrystals). For this sample specifically, no tensile ductility, hardness or fracture data are reported; its significance is as the composition-dependence reference of the study.
mechanisms: Pure iron defines the 0 at.% Al end of the near-linear yield-stress vs Al-content relation: the interpolating straight lines through the polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al data give a hardening rate of 21 MPa per at.% Al at 10⁻² s⁻¹ and 23 MPa per at.% Al at 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, i.e. the reference yield stress fixes the intercept of the solid-solution hardening law.

The linear strength increase with Al content up to 18 at.% Al, of which pure iron is the zero-solute anchor, is attributed exclusively to substitutional solid-solution hardening described by Suzuki's theory for bcc alloys; the overall coefficient for the polycrystalline 0–18 at.% Al alloys is about 2.2 GPa and is not sensitive to deformation rate or temperature.

Because the pure iron was tested as-cast and unheat-treated, it bypasses the quenched-in excess-vacancy mechanism (vacancy hardening and reduced dislocation mobility) that governs the quenched Fe-Al specimens; its absence of a prior high-temperature anneal/quench means no excess vacancies and no ordering-related contribution enter its yield stress.

The high-purity, low-carbon condition of the reference iron suppresses grain-boundary carbide precipitation (such carbides require slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C or long anneals and grow with increasing C content), so its as-cast structure is single-phase and precipitate-free.

The coarse-grained (order of 1 mm) polycrystalline state means the compressive yield stress reflects multiple-slip polycrystal behaviour rather than single-slip geometry, which the paper uses to explain why its derived hardening coefficient (~2.2 GPa) exceeds the ~1 GPa reported for annealed Fe-Al monocrystals.
microstructure: Polycrystalline pure iron with a coarse grain structure; the polycrystalline Fe-Al alloys are reported to show grain sizes of the order of 1 mm, and this pure-iron reference is described as rather coarse-grained, with the tested specimens taken in perpendicular orientations in the original ingot (consistent with a coarse, inhomogeneous cast structure). The as-cast material contained no second phases. Optical metallography after etching in alcoholic 10% nitric acid was used to reveal grain boundaries and precipitates, and it established that fine thin plate-like or rod-like precipitates (believed to be carbides from the residual carbon) appeared only on grain boundaries after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C or prolonged annealing (e.g. 14 days at 320 °C), their amount decreasing with lower C content; the present as-cast, unheat-treated state therefore remains free of such precipitates. No texture, dislocation-density or grain-size-distribution data are reported specifically for this sample.
processing: Route: electron-beam remelting (melting/preparation) → solidified ingot used directly in the as-cast condition → specimen preparation. The pure iron was produced by electron-beam remelting rather than by the vacuum induction melting in Al2O3 crucibles used for the Al-containing alloys (levitation melting was used only for selected alloys). No second processing step was imposed: the material was tested in the as-cast condition with no subsequent heat treatment, in explicit contrast to the annealed/quenched Fe-Al monocrystal specimens of the same study. Specimens were taken with perpendicular orientations in the original ingot. Specimen preparation consisted of electrostatic discharge machining, mechanical polishing and ultrasonic cleaning in acetone; the surfaces of the 5 × 5 × 10 mm³ compression specimens were then cleansed by grinding before testing. No temperature, time, atmosphere or cooling-medium parameters are reported for the remelting itself.
properties: Mechanical behaviour was assessed by uniaxial compression testing at room temperature on 5 × 5 × 10 mm³ specimens, taking the yield stress as the 0.2% proof stress with total straining of at least 5%. The compressive yield stress of pure iron is ~100 MPa at a rate of 10⁻² s⁻¹ and lies between 0 and 100 MPa at 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. The value was obtained by averaging the data for 3 rather coarse-grained specimens with perpendicular orientations in the original ingot; the yield-stress data of the study were reproducible to within 3% at most (usually two specimens per alloy differing by 3% at most). In Fig. 3 the 0 at.% Al open circle (10⁻² s⁻¹) lies on the 100 MPa gridline, while the filled circle (10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) sits between the 0 and 100 MPa lines. No tensile ductility, hardness (HU), fracture or physical/chemical property data are reported specifically for the pure-iron specimen. Characterisation techniques applied within the study (and to its specimens) comprise: inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis for chemical composition; optical microscopy after etching in alcoholic 10% nitric acid for grain boundaries and precipitates; SEM with EDX for fracture surfaces and qualitative precipitate analysis; TEM (Philips CM20, 200 kV; thin foils by twin-jet polishing at −30 °C and 12 V in 7:3 methanol:nitric acid, ion milling if necessary) for deformation dislocation structures; and uniaxial compression testing.
summary: This sample is the polycrystalline pure-iron reference (nominal 0 at.% Al, "pure iron specimens"/"coarse-grained iron specimens") used in Herrmann, Inden and Sauthoff's study of the low-temperature deformation behaviour of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys. It was prepared by electron-beam remelting and tested in the as-cast condition without any subsequent heat treatment. Its role is to act as the 0 at.% Al anchor point for the room-temperature composition dependence of the compressive yield stress, thereby defining the zero-solute origin of the linear solid-solution hardening of the Fe-Al alloys with up to 18 at.% Al, and thus also the baseline against which the effects of Al content, ordering, and quenched-in excess vacancies were judged.
